question: Should every law expire after a fixed period unless lawmakers vote to renew it?
answer: Laws outlive their reasons: duelling oaths and medieval debt rules still stand because nobody is obliged to look. In 2013 Britain needed a single Act to repeal hundreds of dead statutes at once. An expiry date forces a review, a vote and a record of who wanted the rule kept.
move: Whichever side you took, whether lawmakers have time to renew decides it.
ask: Which commitment of mine would I not renew if I had to choose again today?
counterpoint: Expiry creates cliff edges: taxes, contracts and criminal offences lapse if a busy or deadlocked parliament misses a deadline. Renewals then become rubber stamps, as long-running security powers show. People and businesses plan on stable law, and obsolete statutes do little harm because courts and prosecutors simply leave them unused.
reference: Statute Law (Repeals) Act 2013, c. 2, United Kingdom Parliament, 2013
